questions.stem: When a person moves from a bright room into a dark cinema, their pupils dilate (get larger). Which muscles in the iris are responsible, and how do they achieve this?

options.text: The circular muscles contract, pulling the pupil open
The radial muscles contract, pulling the iris outward and making the pupil larger
The ciliary muscles contract, changing the shape of the lens
The suspensory ligaments relax, allowing the pupil to expand

questions.explanation: In dim light, the radial muscles of the iris contract (and circular muscles relax), pulling the iris tissue outward. This makes the pupil larger (dilated), allowing more light to enter the eye and reach the retina. This is an automatic reflex response.

questions.stem: To focus on a nearby book, the eye must accommodate. Which changes occur in the eye during this process?

options.text: Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments tighten, lens becomes thinner
Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, lens becomes thicker and more curved
The cornea changes shape to refract light more
The retina moves closer to the lens

questions.explanation: For near vision: ciliary muscles contract, becoming shorter and fatter. This reduces tension on the suspensory ligaments, which go slack. The elastic lens springs into a thicker, more rounded shape, increasing its refractive power to focus the diverging light rays from a near object.

questions.stem: The retina contains two types of receptor cells: rods and cones. A patient has difficulty seeing in dim light but can see colours normally in bright light. Which receptor cells are most likely affected?

options.text: Cone cells, which detect colour
Rod cells, which are sensitive to dim light
Both rods and cones equally
The optic nerve, not the receptor cells

questions.explanation: Rod cells are very sensitive to light and work in dim conditions but cannot distinguish colours. Cone cells detect colour but need brighter light to function. If the patient struggles in dim light but sees colours normally in bright light, their rod cells are affected while cones function normally.

questions.stem: The cornea is responsible for most of the refraction of light entering the eye, yet we often focus on the lens when discussing vision. Why is the lens important despite the cornea doing most of the refraction?

options.text: The lens produces the light that the eye detects
The lens can change shape to adjust focus for objects at different distances, which the fixed cornea cannot do
The cornea only refracts red light, so the lens is needed for other colours
The lens is larger than the cornea and therefore more important

questions.explanation: While the cornea provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power, it has a fixed shape and cannot adjust. The lens can change shape (accommodation) to fine-tune the focus for objects at different distances — becoming thicker for near objects and thinner for distant objects.

questions.stem: A person has damage to their optic nerve in one eye. What would be the effect on their vision?

options.text: They would see everything in black and white from that eye
They would lose all vision in that eye because nerve impulses cannot travel from the retina to the brain
They would only lose the ability to focus on near objects
They would see double vision from that eye

questions.explanation: The optic nerve carries all visual information as electrical impulses from the retina to the brain. If it is damaged, no signals can reach the brain from that eye, resulting in complete blindness in the affected eye, regardless of whether the retina and rest of the eye are healthy.
